title: Introduction
content: FlowJoe is a local-first visual workspace for branching, reference-heavy work — structure on the left, media on the right, and an AI collaborator that never owns your tree.

title: Introduction
content: Use Search FlowJoe docs at the top of a page, or press ⌘K on Mac or Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux. Type a word or phrase, use the arrow keys to pick a result, and press Enter to open it. Choosing a result closes search so you can read the article. Press Escape to close search and return to your page. On smaller screens, use the search icon in the header. Search covers the published articles and updates when the manual is rebuilt. Results include short excerpts and links to matching sections.

title: Introduction
content: FlowJoe is a local-first, desktop-first workspace built around hierarchical trees called Flows. Each node is a living container: notes, status, theming, and a rich media gallery of images, audio, video, documents, spreadsheets, calendars, URLs, and embeds — with an AI collaborator (Joe) who can see context you allow and propose changes you approve. It is for people doing serious creative, research, or professional work that is branching, relational, visual, and reference-heavy. In FlowJoe the tree is not just an organizer. It is the primary surface for thinking. FlowJoe is not a public HTTP API product. These docs are shaped like modern product documentation — overview, concepts, surfaces, guides, and reference — so you can learn how the app works.

title: Introduction
content: At its heart, FlowJoe is built around three first-class citizens: Idea What you work with Structure The tree — roots, nodes, hierarchy, status, themes References The gallery inside each node — media, stacks, tags, workbenches Meaning Notes, summaries, tags, and the context you give yourself and Joe Structure and visual reference material are designed to coexist without one constantly trying to dominate the other.

title: Introduction
content: One useful way to think about the interface — and about these docs: Structure (left) The tree is order, hierarchy, and place — where everything belongs. Roots, nodes, parents, children, siblings. References (right) The gallery is association and seeing many things side-by-side. Media, stacks, tags, workbenches. The divider between them is your control: more structure or more visual space, whenever you need it. Structure gives the work a place; references hold the material; notes explain why it matters.

title: Introduction
content: Here is how these hemispheres map to the actual FlowJoe application interface: The current Canvas workspace in Modern Ember with Compact density. Many tools force everything into one mode. FlowJoe gives you two strong hemispheres and a direct way to balance them.

title: Introduction
content: Local-first with transparency Your data lives on your machine. Storage usage is visible and cleanable. References are not second-class Media, documents, and URLs are meant to be lived inside of, not just attached. Discovery views stay honest Tag queries and all-node search produce virtual galleries you can explore without accidentally rewriting structure. AI is a collaborator, not the owner Joe proposes; you approve. He never silently rewrites your tree. Scoped safety Undo and history stay local enough that deep work in one area does not create chaos everywhere else. Honest limitations When something is intentionally not supported, the product (and these docs) say so.

title: Install FlowJoe
content: Download FlowJoe for Mac, Windows or Linux, open it the first time, update it and uninstall it. FlowJoe is a desktop app. Download it from flowjoe.app/download. The page suggests the right file for your computer and lists every other one. You don’t need an account to install FlowJoe or to create and edit Flows. An account is only for sharing and paid features.

title: Install FlowJoe
content: Computer File Needs Mac .dmg Apple Silicon (M1 or later), macOS 13 Ventura or later Windows .exe installer Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit Linux .AppImage 64-bit (x86-64), any distribution Intel Macs and a Debian/Ubuntu .deb package are coming before the public launch.

title: Install FlowJoe
header: Install and open it the first time
content: This alpha isn’t signed by Apple or Microsoft yet, so your computer asks you once to confirm before it opens FlowJoe. Signed builds arrive before the public launch. Mac Windows Linux 1 Install Open the downloaded .dmg and drag FlowJoe into Applications. 2 Open it once Open FlowJoe from Applications. macOS says it can’t verify the app; click Done. 3 Allow it Open System Settings → Privacy & Security, scroll down to the message about FlowJoe and click Open Anyway. Confirm with your Mac password if asked. From then on, FlowJoe opens normally. 1 Run the installer Open the downloaded .exe. If you see Windows protected your PC, click More info, then Run anyway. 2 Open FlowJoe FlowJoe installs just for you, with no administrator password, and adds itself to the Start menu. 1 Make it runnable In a terminal, in the folder you downloaded it to, run chmod +x FlowJoe-*.AppImage. (Most file managers can also do this under the file’s Properties → Permissions.) 2 Open it Double-click the AppImage, or run ./FlowJoe-*.AppImage. The first time FlowJoe opens, Joe walks you through a short setup. See Quick Start & Onboarding.

title: Install FlowJoe
content: The download page lists a SHA-256 fingerprint for each file. To check yours matches: Mac or Linux: shasum -a 256 <file> in Terminal Windows: Get-FileHash <file> in PowerShell

title: Install FlowJoe
content: FlowJoe doesn’t update itself yet. To update, download the newer version from flowjoe.app/download and install it the same way, over the old one. Your Flows and settings stay where they are.

title: Install FlowJoe
content: Mac: drag FlowJoe from Applications to the Trash. Windows: Settings → Apps → Installed apps, find FlowJoe, then Uninstall. Linux: delete the AppImage file. Uninstalling removes the app, not your work. Your Flows stay on your computer.

title: Quick Start & Onboarding
content: A walkthrough of your first-run welcome wizard and the interactive coach-mark tour in FlowJoe. When you open FlowJoe for the first time, you are greeted by Joe—your local AI assistant. Joe guides you through a brief, two-minute onboarding flow to set up your first workspace and show you around. Here is what to expect during your first run, and how to get back to those settings later.

title: Quick Start & Onboarding
content: Start with your language, then follow the setup screens to name and shape your first Flow. The onboarding wizard helps you seed your project and select your interface preferences. You can complete setup with the keyboard: use Tab and Shift+Tab to move through the wizard, then press Enter or Space to choose a starting shape or theme. 1 Name your Flow Every project starts with a Flow—the whole document, containing one or more root nodes. Choose a title that matches your current goal, such as Novel Draft, Research Board, or Product Design Plan. 2 Pick a Starting Shape To prevent staring at a blank screen, pick one of our pre-designed outline shapes to seed your tree: Project: Seeds Planning, Tasks, and Assets nodes. Media Library: Seeds Images, Audio, and Video nodes. People / Clients: Seeds Clients, Meetings, and Deliverables nodes. Blank Flow: Seeds a single root node only. Let Joe design it: Type a prompt describing your project (e.g. “Indie game art pipeline”), and Joe will automatically draft a custom outline tree for you. If the request fails or takes more than about 20 seconds, FlowJoe explains that the draft could not be completed and opens a blank Flow instead. Cut-off drafts are not applied. The outline uses the low-cost Luna 6 helper on your OpenAI API key; your later chat-model choice is independent. 3 Optionally Link Joe AI If you want to use Joe’s AI capabilities, you can paste in an OpenAI API key. This unlocks inline image analysis, document summarization, AI artwork generation, and side-by-side spelling/grammar diffs.On desktop, FlowJoe encrypts supported API keys using the operating system’s secure-storage service when available. Browser storage has different protections; see Security & privacy. 4 Choose a Swatch Theme Select a workspace theme color profile that fits your aesthetic: Ember Console: Our signature dark mode with glowing orange/amber accents. Mist Canvas: A warm, paper-toned light mode theme. Violet Focus: A deep dark mode with purple

title: Quick Start & Onboarding
content: Once your flow is created, the app runs a Coach-Mark Tour pointing out the live components of the workspace. If you need to re-orient yourself, here are the 10 spots the tour highlights: After the tour, your Flow grows around your own work. This café launch example shows a populated tree and the selected node’s references in Modern Ember with Compact density. The Flow Tree ([data-spot="tree"]): The left panel outline where your nodes, child nesting, task status dots, and sibling item counts reside. Nodes ([data-spot="node"]): Living containers that store notes, summaries, themes, and their own media galleries. Clicking a node opens its gallery on the right. Gallery navigation: The default Canvas lets you pan, zoom, and arrange cards freely. Use Fit to bring your references back into view; see Gallery layouts. Slots & Media ([data-spot="slot"]): Cards where images, audio, video, PDFs, and web URLs live side-by-side. An action rail sits on the left of each slot card for quick tools. Stacks ([data-spot="stack"]): Drop zones that let you stack alternate versions, revisions, or related assets inside a single slot to keep your workspace tidy. Tags ([data-spot="tags"]): Color-coded labels to tag nodes or media slots. You can query tags to build dynamic search results without breaking your tree structure. Notes ([data-spot="notes"]): Node notes for the big thoughts and slot notes for explaining why a file was saved. Notes persist even if you drag media to a different node. Joe AI ([data-spot="joe"]): The robot icon inside slots and panels to invoke Joe to summarize files, edit code, write notes, or generate illustrations under your approval. Global Audio Player ([data-spot="audio"]): The persistent audio transport in the header. Drag tracks to it to start playlists that keep playing as you move around the tree. Settings ([data-spot="settings"]): The “tuning room” to manage themes, configure API keys, reorder settings cards, run storage cleanups, or export backups.

title: Quick Start & Onboarding
content: Change Themes: You can switch between light, dark, sepia, and cozy themes at any time by going to Settings → Appearance. Edit AI Keys: Update your API keys under Settings → APIs. Run a clean start: If you want to reset your workspace, you can clear app databases from the Settings → Data tab.

title: Structure · References · Meaning
content: The core triad that defines every FlowJoe workspace — how order, reference, and intent work together. Many productivity tools force you into a compromise: you either get a clean text outline with no visual files, or a messy visual canvas where structure is lost. FlowJoe is designed differently. Every workspace is built around a powerful, unified triad: Structure, References, and Meaning. The same three ideas apply whether you are planning a café, a case, a podcast or a game.

title: Structure · References · Meaning
content: Layer The Surface What it Solves What Lives Here Structure The Tree (Left Hemisphere) Where does this live? Hierarchy, nesting, task status, visual branch colors References The Gallery (Right Hemisphere) What am I citing or looking at? Images, audio, videos, PDFs, spreadsheets, calendars Meaning Notes, Summaries & Tags What does this mean for the project? Node summaries, slot notes, cross-cutting metadata

title: Structure · References · Meaning
content: The left side of the app is your Tree. Unlike static folder outlines on your computer, a node in FlowJoe is not just a folder path—it is a living container for your ideas. Nest children as deeply as you need to map out milestones, world-building elements, or research topics. Visual Branch Colors: Highlight parent branches to create distinct zones (e.g. orange for draft phases, green for published chapters).

title: Structure · References · Meaning
content: When you click any node in your tree, its Gallery slides open on the right. This is where your reference material lives. It keeps files, interactive documents, and web links side-by-side without cluttering your outline. Layouts: Arrange references on the freeform Canvas, or switch to experimental Theatre Mode for an immersive review. See Gallery layouts.

title: Structure · References · Meaning
content: Meaning is the intelligence layer you add on top of your raw references. A project is more than just a list of files; it is about intent: Node Summaries: The overarching executive overview of what is happening in a branch. Slot Notes: Annotations attached directly to files explaining why they were saved. Tags: Labels that cross-cut your tree, letting you build dynamic search views instantly. [!TIP] How Joe Leverages the Triad: Joe (your AI collaborator) respects this split. When you ask Joe a question, he reads the Structure to understand your outline, inspects the References (like reading a spreadsheet or analyzing image pixels), and anchors his answer on your custom Meaning (notes and summaries) to write contextually intelligent proposals.

title: Local-first storage
content: Keep your work close, work offline, and take it with you. FlowJoe is a desktop workspace that keeps your tree, notes, and imported media on your computer. You can organize ideas and work with saved references without signing into a hosted workspace. A live Workspace folder and a portable exported copy serve different purposes.

title: Local-first storage
content: Your local outlines, notes, and saved files remain available without an internet connection. Free local audio transcription also works offline after its engine and model are installed. Websites, online AI, remote sharing, and model downloads need a connection. Recurring Joe tasks may contact an AI provider while the owning Flow is open and scheduled runs are enabled.

title: Local-first storage
header: Choose how to store a Flow
content: Local storage: FlowJoe manages the Flow and its media in this computer’s app storage. Workspace Folder: Choose a folder containing the Flow and shared media. You can back it up, sync it with your own service, and use it with external tools. Private content stays on its original computer. See Workspace folders for setup, changing computers, and what happens when another tool changes the folder.

title: Local-first storage
content: Export a .fj package to take the Flow and its included media together, or choose JSON for a data-only copy. Right-click a node to export just that branch or copy its JSON. Linked files need separate attention because their paths may not exist on another computer. See Export & import.

title: Local-first storage
content: Think of FlowJoe as a mobile file explorer for your ideas. A normal folder carries files; a Flow carries the structure that makes those files useful: the outline, reference gallery, notes, connections, and included media. Your research desk, story bible, project archive, or creative studio can travel in your pocket. Put your full .fj packages and a copy of the FlowJoe app or installer for the computers you use on a thumb drive. You can pick up your Flow on a compatible computer without bringing your own laptop, signing into a hosted workspace, or rebuilding your collection of references. The same .fj package can move between supported desktop platforms; use the appropriate FlowJoe build for each operating system and processor.

title: Local-first storage
content: Choose File → Export Flow → Full package (.fj) and save the package to your thumb drive. Select the history you want to include; you can also protect the package with a password. On the other computer, launch or install its compatible FlowJoe app, then use File → Import Flow to open your package. You need permission to run apps on that computer. Explore, organize, and edit your Flow. Included files and local notes are available offline; websites and online AI still need a connection. Before you leave, export the updated full .fj package back to the drive. Keep an earlier copy if you want a recovery point, then close FlowJoe and safely eject the drive. The package is a portable snapshot: opening it does not turn it into a file that FlowJoe continually saves back to your thumb drive. Local storage belongs to the computer you are using, even when the app itself is on a removable drive. Export your changes before moving on. For a working folder that receives saves directly, you can instead keep a Workspace Folder on the drive and connect it through Settings → Data. Keep the drive connected while working and close FlowJoe before ejecting it. Private content in a Workspace stays on its original computer; review what travels before switching machines. Bring the files, not just their paths. Full packages bundle included imported media. Linked local files remain references: copy their originals separately and relink them on the destination computer. A saved website link also needs internet access to load its live content. See Export & import for package choices and password protection, or Workspace folders for keeping a live Flow on a drive.

title: Local-first storage
content: Joe uses a provider you configure. Sharing uses the access you grant to guests. API keys use protected desktop storage when available, with a local browser-storage fallback. See Security & privacy for those boundaries.

title: AI as a collaborator
content: Meet Joe: a partner for thinking, creating, and organizing your workspace. Joe works beside your tree and references. You can brainstorm a project, make sense of a document, compare images, draft a summary, or ask him to turn a rough idea into an organized branch. Read the proposed changes before approving. This diagram explains the process; it is not a fabricated Joe response.

title: AI as a collaborator
content: Choose a Flow, node, or slot as Joe’s target. Give him the material he needs, then ask a question or describe a change. For Flow edits, Joe offers a proposal you can approve, reject, or revise. For example: “Group these research links into Sources and Findings, and write a short summary of each.” You review what he intends before it becomes part of the tree.

title: AI as a collaborator
content: Read documents, spreadsheets, calendars, and images together. Write and refine summaries or slot notes, with a review before replacing your text. Generate artwork and keep variations together in a stack. Organize nodes, tags, and gallery references. Save useful memories for later conversations. Set up recurring work, such as refreshing a research board. Control music while you work. Chat edits normally need your approval. Scheduled tasks and connected agents can apply changes under permissions you choose. See Proposals & approval and Automations.

title: AI as a collaborator
header: Your choice of brain and context
content: Configure a supported API connection or signed-in command-line brain. Joe’s access controls let you choose whether he can read the Flow or propose changes. Private and Hidden-from-Joe content stay sealed; the outline may still show node names and positions. Start with Meeting Joe, Bring Your Own Brain, and Permissions & privacy. To let an outside coding assistant work with the Flow, see Agent Bridge.

title: Plugins & specialized workflows
content: Use FlowJoe for your field today, and understand the future plugin direction. FlowJoe’s mix of structure, references, and Joe works well for projects with a vocabulary of their own: characters and scenes, clients and evidence, experiments and datasets, episodes and takes. You can shape those workspaces today using nodes, tags, summaries, spreadsheets, calendars, and saved Joe memories. See Ways to use FlowJoe for examples.

title: Plugins & specialized workflows
content: A future plugin system is planned to offer specialized fields, ready-made project templates, custom views, and domain-specific help from Joe. For example, a story plugin could add character fields and a story-bible template; a research plugin could organize experiment records. The plugin installer, marketplace, and custom plugin panels are not currently available. These ideas describe future work rather than settings you can enable in today’s app.

title: Plugins & specialized workflows
content: Repo nodes and Git bring code, file editing, branches, and version control into a visual project. Workbenches put editable sheets, documents, and calendars beside your references. Joe can help analyze material and propose changes you review. Agent Bridge connects compatible local AI tools to permitted Flow content. Start with the workspace you need now; no plugin is required.

title: About future plugins
content: What the planned plugin system means for people using FlowJoe today. FlowJoe’s tree, references, and Joe already suit many kinds of work. A future plugin system is planned to add more specialized tools—for example, character fields for a story bible or experiment templates for a lab notebook. The plugin installer, marketplace, and custom plugin panels are not currently available. Proposed plugin formats are design plans, not features you can turn on in Settings. You can build a tailored workspace today using nodes, tags, summaries, spreadsheets, calendars, and recurring Joe tasks. For outside AI tools, the existing Agent Bridge lets a connected agent read permitted content and request reviewed changes. See Ways to use FlowJoe for practical starting points and Plugins & specialized workflows for the direction of future plugins.

title: Ways to Use FlowJoe
content: Discover how different professionals and teams utilize FlowJoe's visual tree and media slots, ordered from professional workflows to creative disciplines. Most database or note-taking tools force your thoughts into flat lists, rows, or linear documents. FlowJoe is built for the branching, visual reality of complex planning and creative thinking. Here are the primary ways users leverage FlowJoe’s split-hemisphere model, structured from Professional & Technical workflows to Creative & Personal disciplines:

title: Ways to Use FlowJoe
content: For product teams, software developers, and AI agents developers. Feature Launch Maps: Branch outlines from a root launch (e.g. Billing, Analytics) down to specifications, checklist tasks, and UI mockups. Workbench Islands: Edit spreadsheet specifications, project calendars, or rich text specs in isolated workbench slots. Agentic Workspaces: Connect the Agent Bridge (MCP) to let terminal-based agents (like Claude Code or custom scripts) inspect your tree outline and propose draft roadmap changes for your approval.

title: Ways to Use FlowJoe
content: For researchers, graduate students, and R&D lab groups. Lab Notebooks: Create child nodes for individual experiment runs, storing step-by-step protocols, calibration files, and lab notes. Literature Mapping: Ingest papers, PDFs, and citations. Link research sources to observed data figures in a single structured layout. Dataset Indexes: Point to massive local CSV/XLSX spreadsheets using linked local files to reference data without bloating your project size.

title: Ways to Use FlowJoe
content: For litigators, estate planners, and compliance officers. Case Folders: Structure cases by client, witness, deposition, and exhibit. Evidence Packets: Store scan PDFs, court transcripts, timeline charts, and audio statements. Security & Privacy: Put confidential witness files or client records into Private Nodes to keep them out of Joe’s context. When an older Flow is opened in a Workspace Folder, FlowJoe preserves private content in owner-only storage and verifies the redacted folder copy before saving resumes. Copies made before migration cannot be recalled; a retained backup that still contains private text gets the same placeholder treatment, and a backup too damaged to check is removed. See Workspace Folders.

title: Ways to Use FlowJoe
content: After Hours keeps music cues, episode planning and edit decisions in separate branches. For podcast hosts, producers, sound designers, and narrative audio teams. Visual Episode Boards: Create a root node for the Show, branch into Seasons, and nest individual Episodes. Inside the episode node, attach guest bio PDFs, research links, and sponsor read copy sheets side-by-side. Sonic Clip Stacks: Stack intro stings, music cues, sound effects, ad reads, and recorded interview drafts inside a single slot to compare takes. Persistent Workspace Playback: Play raw interview files or episode draft mixes in the persistent global player, allowing you to listen to drafts uninterrupted while jumping around the tree outline to add edit notes or timestamps. ID3 Tag Auto-Scraping: Instantly parse incoming MP3/M4A clips to extract titles, artists, and embedded cover art, rendering them as card thumbnails so visual reference audio is instantly browsable. Private recording transcripts: Transcribe interviews and voice notes for free on your computer, even offline after setup. Choose plain text or timestamps; keep paid online transcription available when you need its speaker-label option. Transcribe audio. AI-Assisted Show Notes: Paste interview transcripts into nodes and ask Joe to compile show notes, extract highlight quotes, suggest social media captions, or generate timestamp markers under your approval.

title: Ways to Use FlowJoe
content: For YouTubers, TikTok creators, newsletter writers, and social media managers. Visual Content Calendars: Plan YouTube, TikTok, or newsletter schedules side-by-side using the built-in calendar workbench, setting platform labels (#youtube, #tiktok) and custom visual statuses. Thumbnail & Hook Stacks: A/B test thumbnail designs or script hooks by stacking variations in a single slot, keeping layout previews clean and comparative. Sponsor & Campaign Boards: Map sponsor campaigns, tracking media briefs, deliverables, visual assets, and analytics metrics side-by-side. Platform-Aware Scripting: Write script drafts using the rich document workbench. Ask Joe to generate platform-specific caption variants, write catchy hook options, or outline a repurposing matrix (turning a long video outline into 5 short script concepts). Publishing Checklists: Set up automated interval tasks using Joe Automation to scrape trending references or rotate reference thumbnail image assets.

title: Ways to Use FlowJoe
content: For novelists, children’s book creators, graphic novelists, and publishing editors. Graphic Novel Issue Boards: Structure graphic novel volumes as root nodes, branching down into chapters and pages (Page 1, Page 2, Page 3). Organize individual panels or page drafts in media slots. Visual Panel Stacks (Art Pass Tracking): Keep script drafts, layout thumbnails, penciled lines, ink passes, color revisions, and lettering versions stacked inside a single gallery slot. Use the scrubber to flip between stages of page production. Children’s Book Spread Layouts: Map layout spreads as nodes, putting draft text side-by-side with mock illustrations in the split-hemisphere gallery to maintain layout, typography, and image cohesion. Audio Read-Aloud Cadence: Record read-aloud tests of draft pages. Play them in the persistent header player to verify rhythm and cadence while editing draft text inside a rich document workbench. Book Launch & Cover Art Stacks: Manage manuscript edits, cover mockups, distributor sheets, and promotional assets side-by-side, stacking different cover designs in one place to compare variants. Character Bibles & Continuity: Set up character rosters, location bibles, and model sheets. Use Joe to analyze dialogue passes, write panel description variants, or scan drafts for continuity leaks.

title: Ways to Use FlowJoe
content: Lantern Vale keeps a mechanic’s design and the question to test beside each other. For game developers, wargamers, and board game prototyping. Balance Units: Track units, points costs, and special rules using custom grid systems. Playtest Logs: Set up a dedicated playtest log branch to capture photos of prototype boards, audio session notes, and balance feedback. AI Lore Hooks: Call Joe directly inside a character node’s slot to brainstorm flavor text or generate concept art references.

title: Ways to Use FlowJoe
content: For authors, worldbuilders, and wargame narrative designers. Organize Lore: Set up a root node for the Magic System, Geography, or Historical Timeline, and branch down to individual characters, spell listings, or regional maps. Mood Boards: Drag and drop reference illustrations, character headshots, audio recordings, or clothing samples directly into the slots on relevant nodes. Visual Stacks: Keep multiple iterations of character portrait drafts or dialogue sheets stacked together in a single gallery slot.

title: Ways to Use FlowJoe
content: For family histories, daily journaling, travel planning, or errands. Family Tree Archives: Build branches from grandparents to grandchildren, storing portraits, handwritten letter scans, and voice messages. Travel Journals: Group travel nodes with restaurant screenshots, hotel reservation PDFs, and mapped routing lists.

title: Tree anatomy
content: How a Flow is built: roots, nodes, parents, children, and siblings — the spine of every workspace. The tree is the left side of FlowJoe. It is the spine of a Flow: where things live, how they nest, and how you move around large projects without losing the plot. In this story bible, Regions & places holds locations while Factions & customs holds the groups that live there. Selecting The lantern marsh shows that node’s map and reference notes.

title: Tree anatomy
content: A Flow is the entire workspace document. It is represented by a single tree outline (or a multi-root tree) and encapsulates all of your work: Top-Level Identity: A Flow has its own name, visual theme profile, and executive summary. Dangling Project Nodes: You can organize distinct projects, chapters, research boards, or ideas as separate outline branches dangling off the root. Independent Customization: Each node is an independent “living container.” You can customize every branch individually with its own title, task status (Not Started, In Progress, Completed, or Neutral), protection settings (Frozen or Private), visual themes, and local galleries without affecting the parent outline. Opening another Flow is like opening another project file. Your media and structure travel with it when you export (especially a full .fj package).

title: Tree anatomy
content: A root is a top-level node — nothing sits above it in the tree. Many Flows start with a single root and grow downward. FlowJoe also supports multi-root Flows: several top-level branches side by side (for example separate product lines, or “Work” and “Life” in one document). Roots are still nodes. They can have a gallery, notes, status, and theme like any other node.

title: Tree anatomy
content: A node is a place in the tree. It is not just a label. Each node can hold: A name (and place in the hierarchy) Meaning — notes, a summary, status, theme References — its own gallery of media, stacks, links, and workbenches Think of a node as a living container: “this chapter,” “this client,” “this research thread,” “this milestone.”

title: Tree anatomy
content: Hierarchy is parent → child: Root (or any parent) ├── Child A │ ├── Grandchild A1 │ └── Grandchild A2 └── Child B A parent owns a list of children. A child has exactly one parent in the tree (except roots, which have none). Depth can go as deep as the work needs — outlines, worldbuilding, org maps, multi-phase plans. Creating a child is how you break a big idea into parts without losing the parent as the “home” for shared context and media. Here, The lantern marsh is a child of Regions & places and a parent of Reedhaven and The glass groves. Those two places are siblings because they share the same parent. Each still has its own gallery and summary.

title: Tree anatomy
content: Siblings are nodes that share the same parent (including multiple roots, which are siblings at the top level). Order among siblings matters: you can reorder them to match priority, timeline, or narrative sequence. Bulk actions often target a multi-selection of siblings or mixed branches.

title: Tree anatomy
content: Whatever you select in the tree drives the right side of the app: Select a node → its gallery (and node-level chrome) is what you see. Multi-select → bulk tree actions; the gallery still follows the product’s selection rules for the focused node. The tree is navigation and structure. You are not only browsing a list — you are choosing where the next piece of work lives.

title: Tree anatomy
content: Navigating and selecting Creating, renaming, reordering Gallery anatomy Core mental model

title: Navigating & Multi-Select
content: How to move around, filter, and bulk-edit your FlowJoe tree. The left hemisphere of FlowJoe is the Tree. As your project grows, knowing how to navigate, filter, and edit the tree in bulk keeps you fast and organized.

title: Navigating & Multi-Select
content: You can navigate the tree using either your mouse or standard keyboard shortcuts: Arrow Keys: Use Up and Down to move selection. Left Arrow: Collapse the selected node. Right Arrow: Expand the selected node. Spacebar: Toggle node expansion. Enter or F2 renames a single selected node when you are not typing in a field.

title: Navigating & Multi-Select
content: At the top of the tree panel is a search bar. Typing into this bar filters the tree in real time: Name search: Matching node names stay visible together with their ancestors, so you can see where each result belongs. Filters: Use the tree filter controls for tags, status, visibility, privacy, and frozen state. These are separate from name search. Preserved Collapse State: When you clear the search or close the filter, the tree returns to its exact previous collapse state. You won’t lose your place by quickly checking a keyword. Searching lantern finds a place and a faction in different branches. Their parent paths remain visible, so you can tell where each match belongs.

title: Navigating & Multi-Select
content: For bulk organization, FlowJoe supports select operations: Cmd/Ctrl + Click: Select multiple non-adjacent nodes. Shift + Click: Select a range of adjacent nodes. With multiple nodes selected, you can perform bulk actions: Drag & Drop: Move a group of nodes to a new parent. Bulk Delete: Delete multiple branches at once (with confirmation). Status Change: Mark multiple nodes as “In Progress” or “Done” simultaneously. Theming: Assign color highlights across multiple nodes.

title: Navigating & Multi-Select
content: Right-clicking any node in the tree opens a context menu with essential operations: Add & Sibling Tree Management: Quickly create Child or Sibling nodes, or add a new Root branch. Visibility & Status Toggles: Set status to Not Started, In Progress, Completed, or Neutral, or change protection settings (Hidden, Frozen, Private, Hidden from Joe). Attach Items & Clipboard Media: File-picker shortcuts to attach media assets, or paste clipboard images/videos directly To Start or To End of the node’s gallery without shifting your current selection. Subtree Actions: Easily duplicate nodes, copy raw Node JSON, or export selected subtrees.

title: Navigating & Multi-Select
content: The context menu is designed as a Floating, Draggable Surface. Click the Pin icon in the corner to lock the menu open on the screen, converting it into a persistent floating panel. Drag the panel by its top header to keep a handy command center open while working. Claims System: Pinning a new floating menu (such as the Theme Manager or Tag Manager) automatically closes previously pinned menus to keep your workspace uncluttered. [!WARNING] Nesting Limit: While you can nest nodes as deeply as you need, we recommend keeping your hierarchy structured cleanly. Deeply nested, flat structures can sometimes make sidebar navigation less scannable. Use Summaries to aggregate deep child details!

title: Managing Nodes
content: Add, edit, duplicate, and organize nodes in the hierarchy. Every node in your Flow tree is a container for gallery media, notes, and metadata. Here is how you manage these nodes as your project outline takes shape. Right-click a node to find creation and organization commands in one place.

title: Managing Nodes
content: You can build your tree quickly using keyboard shortcuts or mouse clicks: New node (keyboard): Press N or Ctrl+N. With a node selected, the new node is added as a child. With no node selected, it becomes a root. (On Mac, Cmd+N is New Flow, not add node.) Context Menu: Right-click any node and choose New Node or New Child. There is no Enter / Tab / Insert shortcut for creating siblings or children. Once Add Node is open, use Tab or Shift+Tab to reach Password protect and its lock policies. The timeout field joins that keyboard cycle when shown; hidden fields and disabled actions are skipped. Inside a Private node, Password-protect this node is dimmed with the note “Already protected: this node is inside the Private node “…” and uses its password.” The new node is saved encrypted under that Private node’s password; see One password per Private branch. Cancelling the password step returns to Add Node with your name and privacy choices intact. If another window replaces the password or recovery-key step, node creation is cancelled and the new window stays open.

title: Managing Nodes
content: Quick Rename: Select a node and press F2 or Enter (single selection, tree focus, not while typing in a text field), or double-click the node text to enter edit mode. Save Name: Press Enter or click outside the text box to save the new name. Cancel Rename: Press Escape to revert to the original name.

title: Managing Nodes
content: You can reorder nodes dynamically: Move without dragging: Right-click a node, choose Move Node…, then choose the root, a parent, or a sibling destination. Keyboard users can open the node menu and operate the destination picker without a pointer. Drag and Drop: Click and hold a node to drag it. You can move it between siblings or nest it under a new parent. Drop Indicators: A horizontal bar shows where the node will land if dropped between others. Highlighting a node indicates it will become a child of that node. Subtree Moving: Dragging a parent node automatically moves all of its nested children, preserving the entire sub-hierarchy. Move Node applies the same branch and destination protection rules as dragging. If a move is allowed, the Undo notification can restore the branch to its previous location.

title: Managing Nodes
content: Duplicate Subtree: Right-click a node and select Duplicate. This creates an exact copy of the node, its entire nested child tree, and all associated gallery slots and summaries. Delete: Select a node and press Delete or Cmd/Ctrl + Backspace. Deleting a parent node requires confirmation if it contains children, safeguarding you from accidental data loss. [!TIP] Subtree Exports: You can also export a selected subtree as a standalone .fj file for sharing. See Export & Import to learn more.

title: Status, Themes & Protection
content: Visual status indicators, branch theming, and the four orthogonal node protection states. FlowJoe provides native visual indicators and safety features to help you categorize work, organize outlines, and secure sensitive information.

title: Status, Themes & Protection
content: Every node in FlowJoe can display a status badge. This is useful for project tracking: Status Options: Choose Not Started, In Progress, Completed, or Neutral. Number keys 1–4 set these in that order when the tree has focus. Bulk changes: A parent status change updates editable nodes and skips frozen or password-locked branches. Unlocked siblings still change. The parent badge reflects all children, so a mix of changed and protected children can leave it In Progress. Tree Filtering: Use the tree filter controls to choose a status. The tree search box searches node names. Undo: When Delete Undo (5s) is enabled, Undo after a parent status change restores each child’s previous status, including mixed statuses inside nested groups. The restored values are saved. Joe Awareness: Joe is aware of node statuses and will use them to prioritize suggestions.

title: Status, Themes & Protection
content: To help organize different zones of a large workspace (e.g. distinguishing personal logs from client tasks), FlowJoe supports custom branch themes: Color Coding: Right-click a node, select Theme, and choose a color profile. Inheritance: By default, children nodes inherit their parent’s color theme. This lets you color-code an entire branch (and its gallery slots) in one click. Theme Profiles: Global styling themes (Dark, Light, Cozy, Sepia) are managed in Settings. Joe: You can ask Joe to set a node’s Theme-menu look by its menu name, such as Clay Roast, or ask for a calming, earthy, light, or dark look. He is shown each look’s colors and uses those, not the name alone. A name that is not on the list is refused. Bulk theme clearing: Remove All, resetting node themes to the global theme, and resetting preferences leave frozen or password-locked branches unchanged while clearing editable nodes’ overrides. Clear or app theme: Clearing that look lets the node inherit from its parent again. Asking for the app theme uses the app-wide look on that node and stops inheritance. A frozen or locked Private node refuses the change.

title: Status, Themes & Protection
content: Choose the control for the job; visibility, editability and AI access are separate decisions. FlowJoe supports four independent (orthogonal) node states that can be toggled via the Set Visibility / Privacy… context-menu flyout. These states inherit down the tree, meaning freezing or privatizing a parent applies to the entire subtree. State Purpose Visible? Editable? Secret? Mechanism Hidden Declutter the tree sidebar No (filtered out) n/a until shown No node.hidden boolean toggle Private (password) Access control / privacy No until unlocked No until unlocked Yes (saved encrypted) Node password + temporary memory unlock session Frozen Prevent accidental edits Yes (fully readable) No (read-only) No node.frozen boolean toggle Hidden from Joe Seal content from AI assistant Yes to the human Yes to the human No node.hiddenFromJoe boolean toggle

title: Status, Themes & Protection
content: Hiding a node filters it out of the tree view sidebar without deleting it. To view or edit hidden nodes, toggle Show Hidden Nodes from the tree panel menu. Hidden nodes remain fully editable and unprotected once revealed.

title: Status, Themes & Protection
content: Marking a node as Frozen (padlock icon) keeps its gallery content from being changed by accident. Flows saved earlier with a node “locked” now show that node as frozen, and it works the same way: What is Allowed: You can still reorder/move the node on the tree, copy/export content, and duplicate the branch (the duplicate is created as a new, fully editable, unfrozen sibling). What is Blocked: You cannot rename the node (unfreeze it first), edit slot notes or titles, crop/delete images, reorder or navigate stacks, attach new media, set statuses, or delete the node itself. Unfreeze Toggle: Clicking the padlock badge in the gallery header opens a confirmation modal before unfreezing.

title: Status, Themes & Protection
content: In a password window, Tab and Shift+Tab move through its current controls. Enter activates a focused button, including Cancel and the password reveal button. Escape or Cancel returns to where you opened it; focus stays put if you have moved to another window. Empty or mismatched entries identify the affected field and expose the error to assistive software. When a recovery key is shown, Copy key leaves that window open. If automatic copying is unavailable or refused, select and copy the displayed key yourself. Choose Saved recovery key only after saving it; Cancel protection setup remains available. Private nodes require a password to view their contents in FlowJoe. After unlocking, use normal Joe context, attachments and approved actions; choose Hidden from Joe separately to withhold content from him. Their saved content and media are encrypted and open only with the password. Unlocked, a Private node works like any other node. Everything inside a Private node uses its password: a child can’t have a password of its own, and moving or copying protected content into or out of a Private node asks for its password first; see One password per Private branch. An exported Private node stays encrypted in the file; for a fully protected backup, also enable package password protection; see Password-protected packages. Temporary Unlock: Right-click and enter your password. This starts an in-memory session. Leaving the node, reloading the app, disconnecting the workspace, opening another Flow, starting a New Flow, importing over the current Flow, or restoring a version immediately re-locks it. Workspace Folder privacy: Workspace files show a redacted Private node (not shared) placeholder. When an older Flow is opened, FlowJoe preserves the private content in owner-only storage and verifies the redacted folder file before saving resumes. Copies made before migration cannot be recalled. If a retained backup still contains private text, FlowJoe replaces that text with a

title: Status, Themes & Protection
content: a placeholder (your private notes stay on this computer) and removes any backup too damaged to check; see Workspace Folders. Stays on this computer: A private node’s content stays on the computer where it lives. It does not follow you to your own second computer, even through the same Workspace folder; there it shows only as the placeholder. Removal: To share the node again, choose Remove Password Protection (this requires your password, permanently clears private status, and republishes the node).

title: Status, Themes & Protection
content: Marking a node as Hidden from Joe seals the entire node and its children from the AI assistant: Human View: The node remains fully visible and editable to you. AI Block: Joe cannot read the summary, gallery media, slot notes, or tags of the node. Tool Exclusions: Joe is barred from running mutations, auto-titling, spelling checks, or image generation tools on the node, and the snapshot API emits it as redacted.

title: Node Summaries
content: Durable, high-level context summaries for human clarity and AI grounding. While gallery slot notes describe specific files, the Node Summary field represents the overall meaning of a node in your workspace. For a summary of the whole tree instead of one node, see Flow Summary. A draft worldbuilding summary can separate established lore from unanswered questions. Here, the node summary explains the marsh as a whole; the map’s slot notes describe a particular route.

title: Node Summaries
content: Field Purpose Target Audience Storage Location Node Notes Freeform markdown drafting You (scratchpad, logs) Attached to the Node Node Summary High-level synthesis of status & assets You & Joe (grounding context) Stored as metadata Flow Summary High-level synthesis of the whole tree You & Joe (grounding context) Stored as metadata Slot Notes File annotations You (capturing asset detail) Attached to the Slot

title: Node Summaries
content: Every node has a dedicated summary view that you can open from the top-bar button. It uses FlowJoe’s shared rich-text editor — that page is the full reference for slash commands, the emoji picker, the bubble menu, AI actions, markdown shortcuts, and keyboard shortcuts. Rich-Text Editor: Write and format summaries using an embedded rich-text editor with Markdown storage. Rich Formatting & Dropdowns: Includes quick dropdown toolbars for heading styles (H1–H3, paragraph), text alignments (Left, Center, Right, Justify), advanced marks (Underline, Highlight, Inline Code, Subscript, Superscript), task lists / checklists, tables, blockquotes, and dividers. Slash Commands & Bubble Menu: Type / to insert structural blocks quickly or select text to format on the fly with the floating formatting menu. Undo/Redo: Cmd+Z / Cmd+Shift+Z (and the toolbar’s Undo/Redo icons) walk the same persistent history as the rest of FlowJoe, so your edits are still there to step back through after a reload. Native Right-Click: Right-clicking in the editor opens your system’s standard menu (cut/copy/paste, spelling suggestions, etc.) — dictation and spell-check live on the toolbar here instead. This is specific to summaries and the slot preview view below; gallery slot/stack notes keep their own custom right-click menu. AI actions: Select some text (or just place your cursor in a paragraph) and click ✨ — on the toolbar, or in the floating menu that appears when you select text. Pick Improve, Fix grammar, Simplify, Shorten, Expand, Change tone, Translate, Turn into bullets, Summarize, or Continue writing, or choose Ask Joe… to give any other instruction. The suggestion streams in below your text as Joe writes it, then shows the changes highlighted once it’s done — Stop cancels a request in progress. You can Replace it, Insert it below instead, copy it, tweak it in the box before accepting, or discard it, and Cmd+Z undoes an accepted change. Collapsible Sections & Block Actions: Wrap any selection

title: Node Summaries
content: selection into a collapsible section to tuck away detail, then un-collapse it later while keeping the content. Hover any block for quick duplicate, copy-to-clipboard, and delete actions — plus drag its handle to reorder blocks. Images: Drag an image file straight onto the editor (or paste one) to insert it where you dropped it, or type /upload for a drop box. Click an image to align it, float it so text wraps around it, add a caption or alt text, and drag its corner to resize. Images are stored inside the summary itself, so each file is limited to 4 MB — larger ones are skipped with a notice. Emoji Shortcodes: Type : followed by a name — :fire, :check, :rocket — and pick from the popup. Live Voice Dictation: Dictate summary notes hands-free using FlowJoe’s speech engine, including automatic spoken punctuation and line-break conversion. Brainstorm with Joe: The summary panel has a direct entry point to chat with Joe. You can highlight a draft summary and ask Joe to refine, format, or extract Action Items from it. Spellcheck Review: Built-in review makes editing clean and fast. Open on New Node: A setting toggles whether the summary view automatically pops open whenever you create a new node, encouraging good documentation habits.

title: Node Summaries
header: Why Summaries Matter for AI Context
content: When you chat with Joe, he is given a context bundle. In order to avoid uploading megabytes of raw documents, Joe reads the Node Summaries of the selected node (and, with the default Limit map to my location setting, the outline of this branch rather than the whole tree). A concise summary acts as a directory card that tells the AI exactly what lives in this branch of your project without wasting token budgets. See Token usage with Joe. [!TIP] Summary Compaction: As chat histories grow, FlowJoe can summarize older messages to keep a long conversation going. Saved Joe memories are separate: use Remember this or the Memories panel to keep a fact for later conversations. Writing clear node summaries helps anchor these memories.

title: Node Summaries
content: While you use Summary, Tab and Shift+Tab stay within its window. Text-editor shortcuts, including list indentation, keep their usual meaning. Minimize lets you work elsewhere; restore the window from its pill to continue the same draft.

title: Flow Summary
content: One durable summary for your whole tree, not just a single node. Where a Node Summary captures one node, the Flow Summary captures the whole tree — the single place to write “what this entire workspace is and where it stands” once, instead of piecing it together from individual nodes. The Flow Summary describes the whole archive, while each person’s node summary can describe that branch.

title: Flow Summary
content: Open it from the top-bar button — the same place you’d expect a whole-flow action, distinct from the per-node Summary button that only shows once a node is selected.

title: Flow Summary
content: The Flow Summary uses the same rich-text editor as Node Summary, with the same full toolset: Rich-Text Editor: Write and format the summary using an embedded rich-text editor with Markdown storage. Rich Formatting & Dropdowns: Heading styles (H1–H3, paragraph), text alignments (Left, Center, Right, Justify), advanced marks (Underline, Highlight, Inline Code, Subscript, Superscript), task lists / checklists, tables, blockquotes, and dividers. Slash Commands & Bubble Menu: Type / to insert structural blocks quickly or select text to format on the fly with the floating formatting menu. Undo/Redo: Cmd+Z / Cmd+Shift+Z (and the toolbar’s Undo/Redo icons) walk the same persistent history as the rest of FlowJoe, so your edits are still there to step back through after a reload. Native Right-Click: Right-clicking in the editor opens your system’s standard menu (cut/copy/paste, spelling suggestions, etc.) — dictation and spell-check live on the toolbar here instead. AI actions: Select some text (or just place your cursor in a paragraph) and click ✨ — on the toolbar, or in the floating menu that appears when you select text. Pick Improve, Fix grammar, Simplify, Shorten, Expand, Change tone, Translate, Turn into bullets, Summarize, or Continue writing, or choose Ask Joe… to give any other instruction. The suggestion streams in below your text as Joe writes it, then shows the changes highlighted once it’s done — Stop cancels a request in progress. You can Replace it, Insert it below instead, copy it, tweak it in the box before accepting, or discard it, and Cmd+Z undoes an accepted change. Collapsible Sections & Block Actions: Wrap any selection into a collapsible section to tuck away detail, then un-collapse it later while keeping the content. Hover any block for quick duplicate, copy-to-clipboard, and delete actions — plus drag its handle to reorder blocks. Images: Drag an image file straight onto the editor (or paste one) to insert it where you dropped it, or type /upload for

title: Flow Summary
content: for a drop box. Click an image to align it, float it so text wraps around it, add a caption or alt text, and drag its corner to resize. Images are stored inside the summary itself, so each file is limited to 4 MB — larger ones are skipped with a notice. Emoji Shortcodes: Type : followed by a name — :fire, :check, :rocket — and pick from the popup. Live Voice Dictation: Dictate hands-free using FlowJoe’s speech engine, including automatic spoken punctuation and line-break conversion. Brainstorm with Joe: Highlight a draft and ask Joe to refine, format, or extract Action Items from it. Spellcheck Review: Built-in review makes editing clean and fast.

title: Flow Summary
header: Why It Matters for AI Context
content: The Flow Summary gives Joe a top-level directory card for the entire tree, the same way a Node Summary does for one branch — useful when you want Joe grounded in the shape of the whole project rather than just the currently selected node and its ancestors. It rides with the flow map on each Joe send (the Flow map slice on the token bar). Checking Omit entire flow map leaves both the tree outline and this summary off that send. See Token usage with Joe.

title: Flow Summary
content: While you use Flow Summary, Tab and Shift+Tab stay within its window. Text-editor shortcuts, including list indentation, keep their usual meaning. Minimize lets you work elsewhere; restore the window from its pill to continue the same draft.

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: Keep a project in its own Git repository inside FlowJoe, review changes, create commits, and work with branches and Git remotes. A repo node brings a coding project into the same workspace as its plans, research, screenshots, and conversations with Joe. Browse files, edit several at once, compare changes, make commits, and explore branches without losing the project’s visual context. Folders become child nodes and files become gallery items. Switch between the Canvas and File Explorer to see the project as a reference board or as a code workspace. File saving and Git history are distinct steps; remote synchronization is separate again.

title: Repo nodes and Git
header: A quick tour of the coding workspace
content: What you want to do Where to go Work across several files File Explorer and editor tabs; each file keeps its draft and undo history. See what you changed Diff compares your current file with its last commit. Save a milestone Source Control → Changes: stage files, write a message, and Commit. Explore earlier work Timeline for a file, or Graph for commits and branches. Try a different direction Create a branch and Open Branch as Node to give it a place in the tree. Work with a teammate Share the repository; permitted browser guests use its Explorer, editor, and Source Control through your computer. Save updates the working file. Commit records a chosen set of saved changes in Git history. Push sends commits to the linked remote repository. A repo node is the Git boundary for a project. A Workspace Folder chooses where the whole Flow is stored. They are separate features: do not make the whole Workspace Folder your project repository. See Workspace Folders.

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: Guests use the same Explorer, editor and Source Control surfaces. Can view allows reading shared files and their associated history. Can edit allows creating, editing, renaming, saving and committing shared files through the owner’s computer. Saving and committing are separate actions. Credentials and native filesystem paths stay with the owner, and a scoped commit preserves private and unshared files. The Graph includes branches in the shared repository, including branches not yet open as Flow nodes. A branch represented by a private or unshared node stays unavailable. Guests can read admitted branch history, tags and stashes. Edit guests can create branches and tags, open a branch as a node where that keeps it inside the shared area, merge shared changes, and use Fetch, Pull and Push through the owner’s computer. An Edit guest merges exactly as the owner does, FlowJoe’s notes, layout and history included, and answers FlowJoe’s questions about what they can see. Folders kept from them keep the owner’s version and are never shown to them. An Edit guest can also change a repository’s history choices, and reads and writes the history of the items and folders they can see. Their Changes list shows FlowJoe’s notes, layout and history for what they can see, and their commits write them, as the owner’s do. An Edit guest can run Update Gallery too and answer questions about conflicting changes they can see. It runs on the owner’s computer, so folders kept from them are brought up to date without being shown to them. Discarding working changes, saving a stash that puts files back to their last commit, applying or popping a stash over existing work, rewriting the last commit, renaming or deleting branches, deleting tags or stashes, and replacing or removing a remote require the owner’s additional removal permission. Linking a new remote does not. Private and unshared file contents stay protected when changes are merged, pulled, committed or restored. A guest push stops if

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: if the branch or tag history contains private or unshared files, because Git would send that history to the remote. Fully shared repositories can be pushed normally. A partially completed stash operation reports that some files could not be changed; the saved stash remains available. Removing your own created file requires no extra removal permission when it has no protected contributions from others. Removing someone else’s file requires the owner’s additional removal permission. Editing its text does not make you its creator. Private content remains unavailable with either permission. See Sharing, Guests and Presenting.

title: Repo nodes and Git
header: Create or open a repo node
content: Create, clone, and import repositories in the desktop app. A standalone browser session cannot run native Git; invited guests use the owner’s shared repository tools. Use the New Node window to create an empty repository or clone from a Git remote. To import an existing local Git folder, drag the folder onto the Flow tree and choose Import as Repository. (The other choice, Import as Ordinary Folder, brings it in as a normal folder.) A repo node is the Git boundary for that project: folders become child nodes and files become gallery items. FlowJoe keeps the bare Git history in its own hidden storage and saves the working files through the Flow’s normal storage. It does not create a checkout folder elsewhere on your computer, and it does not put the whole Flow into Git. For a remote, use its HTTPS address or, on macOS and Linux, either SSH form shown by the Git host, such as https://host/owner/project.git, ssh://git@host/owner/project.git, or git@host:owner/project.git. FlowJoe uses one remote named origin for each repo node. A repository imported from a local Git folder can keep its existing SSH origin on macOS and Linux. On Windows, SSH addresses are not supported yet: use an https:// address instead. When you open a repo node, choose Source Control in the app rail. The repository appears with its current branch and any changes waiting to pull or push. The panel is available to the owner and to browser guests with repository access. View guests read shared files and history; Edit guests save and commit through the owner.

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: An Edit guest can make a shared branch a repository through the owner’s computer. The owner’s complete branch is converted, including folders hidden from the guest; those folders are never shown to the guest. Private folders stay home. Names that need fixing are fixed on the owner’s computer. Any branch of your tree can become a repository: right-click its top node and choose Make This a Repository… in the menu’s Organize section (desktop app or an Edit guest using the owner’s computer). Nothing changes until you confirm. A window shows first: What goes in: how many nodes, files and links. Every node becomes a folder, every item becomes a file (pictures and documents as they are, a link as a .url shortcut), and FlowJoe’s small hidden files keep titles, notes, order, canvas layout, themes, tags and automations (switched off for anyone who clones). What stays on this computer: where you are scrolled and zoomed, and your app-wide fonts, text size, line spacing and density. A linked file (one that points at a file elsewhere on your computer) stays here too. Private nodes: Private nodes stay out of repositories. Each one is listed dimmed with a lock and can’t be ticked, and everything inside it stays out too. Git keeps everything as ordinary, readable files, so a Private node never goes in. If you want something included, remove its protection first; it then goes in like any ordinary node. A Private node, or anything inside one, can’t be made a repository either: Make This a Repository… is dimmed on it in the node menu. History: the same choices as .fj export, all off to begin with: Include AI chat and image history (your Joe chats and the pictures Joe made), Include picture prompts (the prompt that made each AI picture), Include Transcript History (kept transcripts and their edits), Include undo notes history (the undo and redo steps of notes, titles and summaries) and Include Memories (what Joe remembers about these nodes and items, and the Flow’s own Memories). See

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: See History in the repository. The repository remembers these choices, and so does every copy someone clones. Names to fix first: in a repository a title is also its file or folder name, so two titles that would clash (capitals don’t count) or a title with characters files can’t have are listed with a suggested name. Accept Fixes and Make Repository renames them (each rename can be undone like any other) and then makes the repository. To pick your own names, cancel, rename them, and start again. Where it goes: Keep it on this computer for now, or Link a GitHub repository with its link (or owner/name). Linking only connects it; push from Source Control when you’re ready. Make Repository makes the first commit straight away, signed with your Git name like any other commit, and Source Control shows the new repository with nothing left to commit. Undo turns it back into an ordinary node. A branch that already holds a repository can’t become one (a repository can’t hold another one). FlowJoe says which repository is inside it and offers Show to select it, so you can move it out first or choose a different branch.

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: Joined guests use the same Explorer and Source Control through the owner’s computer. View reads shared files and history; Edit saves and commits. Elevated removal is required for actions that discard work or rewrite history. Private files and branches stay excluded. The supported actions are described under Shared repositories above. Choose Switch to File Explorer in the repository gallery to show its folder tree and editor. Select a file row to open it in the workbench. Resize the Explorer divider by dragging it or using the keyboard, and use the file tabs to move between files. Each file keeps its own draft and undo history while you switch tabs. Choose Switch to Canvas to return to the repository’s normal gallery. Paths are relative to the repository root (.), such as src/main.js; FlowJoe does not create a checkout folder on your computer. From a folder or the Explorer background, use New File…, New Folder…, or Quick Open…. New File and New Folder place a name field in the Explorer at the target directory. Press Enter to create it; Escape or leaving the field cancels. Name or save errors stay beside the field so you can correct the name. A folder menu can copy that folder’s relative path; the root/background menu has no path to copy. New files need a supported text extension. The editor toolbar has Save, Diff, Find, Format, and word wrap; the active FlowJoe theme applies to the editor. Undo and redo are available through the editor’s standard commands. Diff compares Last commit on the left with the editable Current file on the right, including unsaved edits. Save writes the current file to repository working content and updates Source Control; it does not create a Git commit. To commit, go to Source Control → Changes, stage the files you want, enter a message, then choose Commit. A historical revision is read-only. Restore This Version… copies that revision into the current working file; it does not create a commit. For JavaScript and TypeScript, nearby

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: nearby repository files can help the editor offer suggestions. The workbench does not run your project or provide every service of a standalone development environment. Renaming a branch or changing its remote keeps open editor drafts available. Stash, Pop, Apply, and Close Branch Node ask you to save or discard unsaved editor work before changing files; Cancel keeps your work in place. If you discard a folder deletion, FlowJoe restores its recorded folder protection and creator information along with the files, including after reopening the Flow on this computer. Restoration stops if that information is unavailable, a path now belongs to something else, or a protected folder is locked.

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: The Changes section lists files that differ from the last commit. Its menu offers View as Folders to group the list by folder and Open Changed Files to open every changed file. Stage the files you want to include, write a commit message, then choose Commit. Generate can draft a message from the changes. Generate and Joe reviews leave out Private and Hidden-from-Joe file contents, including protected folders; unlocking a Private folder for yourself does not share it with Joe. You can also review a changed file before committing, discard a change, or use the split button for commit-and-push or commit-and-sync actions.

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: A Private (password-protected) folder inside a repository stays on your computer. Its files appear in Changes under Private · stays out of commits: you can open them, but they are never staged or committed, and pushing never sends them. A file that was committed before its folder became Private stays at that committed version. If commits made earlier already include files from a Private folder and haven’t been pushed yet, Push stopped explains what was found and offers Remove Them and Push. FlowJoe rewrites only those unpushed commits without the Private files (tags on them move along), then pushes; your files stay on this computer. Merging a branch that changed a file in a folder you later made Private doesn’t stop the push: the merge keeps your version. Nothing changes if FlowJoe can’t reach the remote to check what it already has. Push Tags also stops if a tag points at an unpushed commit with Private files. A branch opened as its own node follows the same Private folders.

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: Git keeps everything as ordinary, readable files, so a repository can’t be password-protected. Make Node Private is dimmed on a repository, and on a node that holds one; the note names the repository, and you can move it out first and then protect the rest. In Add Node (and Add Repository or Clone from GitHub in Source Control, which open the same window), Create as a repository is dimmed inside a Private node, and choosing Root or a place outside it brings it back. Create as a repository and Password-protect this node can’t be ticked together: ticking one dims the other, with a note saying why. Moving a repository into a Private node is refused, and FlowJoe says why; the node stays where it was. A copy (paste or duplicate) of a repository is always ordinary folders and files, so it can go anywhere. Importing a .fj file that holds a repository into a Private node stops before anything is imported: the window names the repository and offers Import at Root Level, where it stays a repository, or Cancel. A file whose own Private node holds a repository can’t be imported as it is; the window says to move the repository out, or remove that node’s password, where the file was made. Joe gets the same answers.

title: Repo nodes and Git
header: Importing a file that holds a repository
content: FlowJoe never quietly changes a repository you import. When a .fj file (opened from the File menu or dropped on the tree) would change what one of its repositories is, nothing is imported until you choose: Into another repository: Git can’t keep one repository inside another. Import as Files adds its folders and files to the repository you chose, and it stops being a repository; Import at Root Level keeps it a separate repository; Cancel imports nothing. A repository inside another repository in the file itself: Import as Files keeps the outer one a repository and brings the inner one in as its folders and files, or Cancel. A repository that is already in this Flow: two nodes can’t share one repository. Import as Files brings in a copy of its folders and files that isn’t a repository, or Cancel. Into a Private node: see above; Import at Root Level or Cancel. New files added through the repo node’s gallery appear in Changes so you can stage them. Imported executable-permission changes also appear, even when the file text is unchanged.

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: Besides your files, a commit can record what you arranged in FlowJoe, so teammates who clone the repository see the branch the way you made it. Each folder with something FlowJoe-specific to say gets one small hidden file (.flowjoe-node.json, plus .flowjoe-repo.json at the top). It holds: folder titles, node summaries, status, and slot and stack notes, the order of slots and folders, the gallery layout, a chosen canvas arrangement and where you placed slots on the canvas, slot colours and connections, tags on nodes and slots (each tag travels with its name, colour and description), placeholder slots, and which picture a stack shows, automations, which arrive switched off on the other computer. Where you are looking on the canvas stays with you. Your Joe chats, picture history, transcripts, undo notes history, Memories and picture prompts stay with you too, unless the repository includes them (see below). A plain code repository gets no FlowJoe files until you add something like a note. A folder with no files is kept in Git through its FlowJoe file.

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: A repository can carry the history around its items, the same history a .fj export can carry. Each kind is a separate choice, and each starts off: Choice What goes in Include AI chat and image history Joe chats about each slot and node, and the pictures Joe made, with their pictures Include picture prompts the prompt that made each AI picture Include Transcript History kept transcripts and their edits Include undo notes history the undo and redo steps of notes, titles and summaries Include Memories Memories saved on a node or slot, and the Flow’s own Memories You choose when you make a branch a repository. To change the choices later, open Source Control, choose … on the repository row, then History in This Repository…, and Save (an Edit guest can too). Turning a choice off stops adding new history. What is already committed stays in the repository’s history, because Git keeps everything it has recorded. What goes in, and what doesn’t: History travels with its item. Each item’s history is kept beside its folder, in a hidden .flowjoe-history folder that FlowJoe never shows as a folder or slot. When the item moves, its history moves with it. When the item is removed, its history is removed too. Stays on this computer: a conversation or transcript you marked to keep on this computer, and everything in a Private folder. A Flow-wide Memory made from a chat in such a folder (or in a Private node elsewhere in the Flow) also stays here. Someone who clones gets the history on the same items, as their own copy. A Flow-wide Memory arrives as a Memory of the repository node, so it doesn’t spread across their whole Flow. Open Branch as Node copies the history into the new node, as Duplicate does, and your Flow’s own Memories are not copied twice. Two people’s history is always kept. When you merge or update the gallery, both sides’ messages, transcripts and Memories are kept, in date order, and the same message is never doubled. FlowJoe never asks a question about history. If

title: Repo nodes and Git
content: If the same Memory or transcript was edited in two ways, both versions are kept. Deleting removes it. Delete a chat, a message, a transcript or a Memory, and your next commit takes it out of the repository; teammates lose it too when they update their gallery. If a teammate changed that same entry in the meantime, their version is kept. Past commits still hold it, as they hold any deleted file. Pictures stored with Git LFS. If the repository sends pictures to Git LFS, a history picture that arrives as an LFS file is not downloaded with the history: the entry keeps naming it and nothing is lost. Update Gallery brings a teammate’s new history in, and takes out what they deleted, even when nothing else changed. Its Undo puts the gallery back, but history that arrived stays with you. Undo of a clone or of Open Branch as Node takes the history that came with it away again.

title: Repo nodes and Git
header: Everything you add becomes a file
content: In a repository, everything in a gallery is committed as a file that opens outside FlowJoe too, and comes back as the same kind of slot when someone clones the repository: In FlowJoe In the repository A link Title.url, an ordinary internet shortcut A spreadsheet, rich document or calendar Title.fjsheet, Title.fjdoc or Title.fjcal: FlowJoe’s own file, the same data a .fj export carries A calendar event Title.fjevent A picture you generated, pasted or copied in the picture file itself (its prompt stays with you unless the repository includes picture prompts) A placeholder nothing extra: it lives in the folder’s FlowJoe file When you edit a spreadsheet, document, calendar or link, its file changes too and shows in Changes. These files are written from their slots, so the file editor shows them read-only: change a link’s address or a spreadsheet in its own slot. The first time you open Changes in a repository you cloned or made before this, its links and other items show up once as new files. Every node inside a repository node is a folder: a node you add, or move in from elsewhere in the tree, gets a folder named after its title. If a node made before this already holds files, they move into its own folder, so your next commit shows them as renamed. A folder you move in from another repository keeps its files as they are (executable scripts and symlinks included), and a folder you move out and back in comes back unchanged. Undoing such a move puts everything back as it was. If a moved-in file’s picture or bytes aren’t on this computer, it stays out of commits and Changes says so. Discard Changes, stashes and Pop bring a link, spreadsheet, document or calendar back as itself. Limits: a linked file (one that points at a file elsewhere on your computer) stays on this computer and is not added; Changes says so in a line under the list. A Private node you move in stays out of every commit and push, as any Private folder does. A virtual slot is a pointer to its original, so

title: Repo nodes and Git
header: Everything you add becomes a file
content: so only the original is a file. Automation slots aren’t committed yet.

title: Repo nodes and Git
header: Titles are file and folder names
content: In a repository a title is also its file or folder name, as in a code editor. Renaming a node in the tree renames its folder, and everything inside moves with it; renaming a file slot renames its file. If you leave off the extension, FlowJoe keeps it: retitling photo.png to “Hero” names the file Hero.png. Git records these as renames, and notes stay with the renamed files. A folder that holds a locked Private folder can’t be renamed or moved to another folder until you unlock it, because the Private folder’s files have to move with it. A name that another file or folder beside it already has is refused, even with different capitals (“Notes” and “notes” are the same name on macOS and Windows), and so is a name with characters files can’t have, such as : / \ * ? " < > |. FlowJoe tells you why and keeps the old name, the same way from the tree, a slot’s title and the Explorer.
